column1: # Hosted platforms that leaked the secrets people stored on them. Section 5 shows one row each.
# One line each, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   id        an id from data/incidents.tsv; its name is what the shared fix names
#   commands  commands on PATH that mean it is used, separated by spaces, or -
#   paths     files or folders that mean it is used, separated by ; (a folder ends in /), or -.
#             The same path tokens as data/sessions.tsv: ~ is the home folder, {AS}, {XDG_DATA}...
#   found     the row's word when it is found: installed, or CLI found
#   advice    the line shown under the row when it is found
#   summary   the summary row when it is the only platform found
# OpenCode: its post on X (data/incidents.tsv's source), and its co-founder's that keys kept in the CLI never
# come to OpenCode. Railway and Zeabur: their disclosures, in Zeabur's words "replace every password and
# key stored on Zeabur" and "revoke old keys with the provider first".

column6: OpenCode emailed the Console users its breach hit, and says those it did not email were not affected. If you got that email, rotate every provider key you saved in the Console. Keys kept only in the CLI never reach OpenCode.
column7: OpenCode found: got its breach email? Rotate keys

column6: Railway asked all users to rotate every environment variable stored there, including API keys and private registry credentials, and to review their logs for unusual activity.
column7: Railway CLI found: rotate secrets stored there

column6: Zeabur said on 19 October that an attacker read the service environment variables stored on the platform, and asked users to replace every password and key stored there. Revoke each old key at its provider first.
column7: Zeabur CLI found: rotate secrets stored there
